topics.title: My History and Future
topics.text:
Hey AoPS community,

This is an alt. account btw to maintain privacy. I am currently in high school, but I thought this applied slightly more here. In 5th grade I joined my school's math team along with my older brother (1 grade above me). I hadn't put much time into math in school, and no time outside of school. I enjoyed the experience of trying problems but I still didn't work on competitive math outside of school. I saw my brother participate in MathCounts and thought that it seemed interesting and wanted to do it as well. In sixth grade, I switched to a larger, but better and more competitive school. This school had a couple fairly smart people and also had an active math team, which I joined. Fast forward to January of my 7th grade year, I still hadn't put very much time into comp. math outside of school, but I had halfheartedly taken 1 AoPS class. I ended up making the school chapter MathCounts team, placing 9th in the school test. I went to chapter, and with a bit of luck, and practice, ended up making state as an individual. I live in Texas by the way so I knew I had no chance of nats or countdown. I practiced a little before state and ended up failing. Didn't get a score, but not in the released names. In 8th grade, I spent a little bit of time before the school competition practicing, but didn't make the top 4 team due to a ton of sillies. Before chapter, I thought that I had state in the bag and so only practiced a little (dumb, I know). At chapter, I did pretty well on target (missed 1, and had 1 silly, so 6 correct), but kinda messed up on target (only got 23). I ended up getting beat for the last individual spot by 1 point. I was pretty upset. In my last year of MathCounts, I got overconfident and missed state by 1 point to a 7th grader from my own school. After that, I did a lot of tests (AMC 8, MathCounts, AMC 10). I got better, but was still very upset about missing state. From AoPS, camps, and other things I knew a lot of people at state and a couple people in cd. Despite not going, I got texted what happened. When this happened, I just though about whether or not to invest a lot of time into comp math (mainly into AMC 10 and AIME). I practiced a decent bit of AMC 10 over summer. I ended up failing AMC 10 and AIME in terms of not meeting my expectations. I took a break from practicing and decided to ask yall about what you think I should do. Should I continue? Quit (aka take the tests with minimal practice)? I feel like these tests require a foundation of knowledge (the volume 1 books and stuff), which I don't have. I feel like starting late, my mind is pretty bad at creatively solving problems and hasn't developed into a good problem solving brain. I also feel that, from school and other stuff, I take longer than most do to learn new concepts. All of these reasons are just really making me debate continuing with comp. math as a part of my life, and I wanted to hear yall's theories about it.

PS: If you have any encouraging stories about people like me that ended up doing ok on oly math later in high school, I would appreciate those.

topics.title: 1st REUN Mock Middle School Math Contest
topics.text:
Hello! This is the 1st REUN Mock Middle School Math Contest. This is a 25-question contest that is designed for middle school students. The questions get progressively harder as you go, so you should expect #25 to be harder than #15. To submit, please send a private message to me with all of your answers. Discussion is allowed on this page, and you can comment things such as 'omg plz sire halp #25!!!11!!.' Just don't expect an answer. Be sure NOT to post answers and solutions on this thread. Private message me the answers



DEADLINE IS NEXT WEDNESDAY AT 3:00 EDT!





Rules:



- All fractions and radicals must be in simplest form. For example, putting $\frac{4}{6}$ as an answer is incorrect; $\frac{2}{3}$ is correct because it is in simplest form. $\sqrt{75}$ is incorrect, however $5\sqrt{3}$ is correct.





Submissions:



- All submissions are valid as long as they have been submitted within 24 hours. In other words, as long as the winners thread has not been posted yet, your submission is valid.



- Please make sure to send a private message containing all of your answers to me.



Point Distribution System:



- The whole test will be scored out of 50 points. An incorrect answer is worth 0 points. An omitted question is worth 1 point. A correct answer is worth 2 points.



- Tiebreakers are determined depending on the question number that was missed. For example, if person A and person B received the same score, but person A missed number 14 and person B missed number 25, person B is the winner of the tiebreaker.



Without further ado, here are the questions:



Click to reveal hidden text1. Compute $5^2-3^2$.



2. What is the units digit of $5^{2016}+5^{2015}$?



3. A circle has a diameter of 5 inches. What is its area, rounded to the nearest whole number?



4. If $g(x) = x^2-x$, what is $\frac{g(100)}{2}$?



5. Joseph can piece together 10 puzzles in 5 minutes. His wiser brother, Matt, can piece together 60 puzzles in 20 minutes. If they work together, how many puzzles can they piece together 4 hours, assuming they work nonstop?



6. Five of the interior angles in a hexagon are 120 degrees, 130 degrees, 125 degrees, 135 degrees, and 105 degrees. What is the sum of the digits of the last interior angle?



7. Find the roots to the equation $x^2-12x=36$.



8. 5 birds can eat 5 biscuits in 5 minutes. How long does it take for 1500 birds to eat 1500 biscuits?



9. Compute $(1+2+3+...+50)+(2+4+6+8+...+100).$



10. A circle is divided into 36 equal sections. If the diameter of the circle is 12, what is the area of 3 of the sections?



11. What is the sum of the factors of 408?



12. If $2(2^2)+2^3+2^4+2^5=2^x,$ what is x?



13. Express $2121_{10}$ in base 5.



14. The volume and the surface area of a sphere are equal to each other. What is the sphere's diameter?



15. The number 900 has x factors. What is $\frac{x!}{(x-2)!}$?



16. You have a dozen Easter eggs for an Easter egg hunt. The eggs come in brown, white and yellow. You want at least one of each color. How many combinations of a dozen eggs are possible?



17. 27 students each flip a fair coin. What is the probability that there are more tails than heads?



18. A cone and a hemisphere that have an equal surface area each have a 6-inch diameter. What is the height of the cone? Express as a radical in simplest form.



19. What is the area of a triangle with side lengths 7, 12, and 15? Express as a radical in simplest form.



20. The sum of the positive multiples of 11 less than 100 can be expressed as x. What is $\frac{x^2-9}{498}$?



21. What is 3 + $\frac{1}{3^1}+\frac{1}{3^2}+\frac{1}{3^3}+\frac{1}{3^4}...$?



22. Express $222_8$ in base 4.



23. Values x and y are the two roots of the equation $5x^2-35x=-10.$ What is $(x+3)(y+3)?$



24. Billy has the frustum of a solid right circular cone. The upper base has a diameter of 6, the lower base has a diameter of 8, and the height is 6. What is the volume of the frustum of Billy's solid right circular cone? Leave pi as is.



25. What is the greatest prime factor of $3^{12}+2^{10}?$

topics.title: A (Serious) Message to Those Who Come in 5th at MC States
topics.text:
Hello everyone. To those who come in 5th at MC States, here is a message. First of all, MATHCOUNTS has no impact on you after May 11, when the Nationals end. There is just a 5 day trip involved, and you may be able to do something even more enjoyable than taking a test if you do not make it. Also, if I did not convince you that coming in 5th is not a big deal, think of it this way. If you come in 5th, then 4 other people make it to Nationals. If you make it to Nats, then one less other person goes, and they have to deal with the "burden" of coming in 5th. Instead, if you come in 5th, an extra person gets to go to Nationals, and you can realize how small of a deal it is. That almost seems like the best possibility!



Note: I would still like a top 4 slot, and I am not saying you should throw the test to get 4 other people to Nats.



Good luck to all!

topics.title: Algebra Help
topics.text:
Could you please help me solve the following question? I'm having difficulty progressing through it.

$a^2 + ab + b^2 = 1\:\:\:\:\:(1)$

$ab-a^2-b^2 = t\:\:\:\:\:(2)$

What is the range of $t?$

I have gotten some things, but they don't seem to be correct

I added $(1)$ and $(2)$: $2ab = 1+t\:\:\:\:\:(3)$

I changed $(2)$: $a^2 + b^2 - ab = -t\:\:\:\:\:(4)$

I added $(1)$ and $(4)$: $2a^2+2b^2 = 1-t \longrightarrow a^2+b^2= \frac{1-t}{2}\:\:\:\:\:(5)$

Adding $(5)$ and $(3)$: $a^2+2ab+b^2 = \frac{3+t}{2} \longrightarrow (a+b)^2 = \frac{3+t}{2} \longrightarrow t = 2(a+b)^2 - 3 \longrightarrow t \ge -3$ due to $(a+b)^2$ always being greater than 0

Then, to find the upper bound, I manipulated $(1)$ and $(2)$

$(a+b)^2 -ab = 1$

$(a - b)^2 + ab = -t$

Adding them, I had $1-t = (a - b)^2 + (a+b)^2 \longrightarrow t = 1-((a-b)^2+(a+b)^2) \longrightarrow t \le 1$ because the sum of squares term is always at least 0, meaning the maximum is 1. However, when I showed my dad this, he said that it was incorrect. Could someone tell me where I went wrong?

topics.title: Math Kangaroo question
topics.text:
I don't get this solution:



A group of 25 people consists of knights, serfs and damsels. Each knight always tells the truth, each serf always lies, and each damsel alternates between telling the truth and lying. Thus, if a damsel answers truthfully to a question, she will always lie on the next question, and tell the truth again on the question after that.



When each of the 25 persons was asked: "Are you a knight?", 17 of them said "Yes".



When each of them was then asked: "Are you a damsel?", 12 of them said "Yes".



When each of them was then asked: "Are you a serf?", 8 of them said "Yes".



How many knights are in the group?

(A) 4 (B) 5 (C) 9 (D) 13 (E) 17



SolutionIt is important to understand that damsels are consistent in their answering at individual level, not as group.



In other words, we need to split the group of damsels into those who start answering by telling the truth and



those who start by telling a lie.



Those who answered YES to the third question were only the lying damsels. So there are at least 8 damsels.



Those who answered YES to the second question were the serfs and the truth-telling damsels. So there are



at most 12 serfs.



Those who said YES to the first question where all but the truth-telling damsels. So 8 damsels replied



truthfully to the first questions, and 8 lied to the third question.



That means there must have been 16 damsels, 4 serfs, and 5 knights.



The answer is (B) 5.
